prompt_free_text:
This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for desktop GUI automation with multimodal LLMs. The core proposal combines three ingredients: hierarchical manager-worker planning, retrieval from both external web knowledge and internal memories, and an Agent-Computer Interface that exposes a language-centric observation/action abstraction over screenshots plus accessibility trees. Empirically, the paper reports a substantial improvement over the OSWorld baseline and additional gains on WindowsAgentArena without explicit adaptation. Overall, I found the paper timely, practically relevant, and reasonably well engineered. The benchmark gains are meaningful for an area where absolute performance remains low and incremental improvements are difficult. At the same time, several aspects of the methodology and evaluation need sharper clarification, and some of the claimed novelty should be stated more carefully relative to prior retrieval-augmented and cognitive-architecture-style agents.

The main strength of the paper is that it tackles an important systems problem in a coherent way. GUI automation is difficult because it requires long-horizon planning, grounding in messy interfaces, and adaptation to application-specific conventions. The proposed decomposition into manager-level planning and worker-level execution is intuitive and well aligned with the structure of the task. The distinction between narrative memory for full-task abstractions and episodic memory for subtask-level action guidance is also sensible. In particular, the idea of storing summarized successful and failed trajectories at different granularities is a useful design choice, and the paper does a good job motivating why full trajectories may be too noisy or brittle for direct reuse. The ACI component is also practically important: constraining the action space to language-level primitives and using accessibility-tree IDs for grounding is likely a major reason the system is more stable than coordinate-only approaches.

The empirical results on OSWorld are the strongest part of the submission. Improving overall success from 11.21% to 20.58% is a large absolute gain for this benchmark, and the category-wise improvements, especially on Daily and Professional tasks, are compelling. The WindowsAgentArena transfer result is also encouraging because it suggests the framework is not narrowly overfit to one benchmark or one OS. The ablations are directionally useful and support the claim that web knowledge, memory, ACI, and hierarchical planning all contribute. I also appreciated the inclusion of error analysis; even though the taxonomy is somewhat coarse, it helps identify where the remaining bottlenecks lie.

That said, the paper is more of a strong integration/system paper than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution. Most of the ingredients have clear precedents: hierarchical planning, retrieval-augmented prompting, reflective trajectory summaries, accessibility-tree grounding, and constrained action spaces have all appeared in adjacent agent literature. The contribution is therefore primarily in how these pieces are combined and adapted to desktop control. That is still valuable, but the novelty claims should be calibrated accordingly. For example, the “experience-augmented hierarchical planning” mechanism appears to be a fairly natural composition of web retrieval, memory retrieval, and manager-worker prompting, rather than a new learning algorithm. Similarly, the “self-supervised continual memory update” is closer to online accumulation of self-generated summaries than to a principled continual learning method. I would encourage the authors to frame the work as a carefully designed architecture with strong empirical validation, rather than implying a deeper methodological advance than is demonstrated.

A more serious concern is evaluation rigor around memory construction and possible benchmark contamination. The paper states that initial memory is bootstrapped through self-supervised exploration using tasks generated from applications used in OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena, and environment-aware tasks are generated from the initial environments of tasks in those benchmarks. This raises an important question: how much information about the test distribution, or even specific test states, is implicitly injected into the memory before evaluation? If exploration uses initial environments derived from benchmark tasks, then the setup may not be strictly zero-shot with respect to the benchmark. Even if the generated tasks differ from the benchmark instructions, the agent may still benefit from exposure to the same applications, layouts, and states. This does not invalidate the results, but it does materially affect how they should be interpreted. The paper needs a much clearer separation between training/exploration data and evaluation data, and ideally should report results under stricter protocols: for example, memory built without using benchmark initial states, memory built only from unrelated applications, or evaluation with frozen memory constructed from an external corpus.

Relatedly, the continual memory update during inference complicates interpretation of the reported benchmark numbers. If the agent updates memory as it processes evaluation tasks, then later tasks may benefit from experience gathered on earlier test tasks. This is a legitimate online-learning setting, but it is not the same as independent per-instance evaluation. The paper should explicitly state whether benchmark tasks are processed sequentially with persistent memory across the test set, whether task order is fixed or randomized, and whether reported numbers are averaged over multiple orders. Without this, it is difficult to compare fairly against baselines that may not have access to cross-instance adaptation. At minimum, the authors should report a “frozen-memory, no test-time updates” condition alongside the online continual-learning condition.

There are also several missing details that matter for reproducibility and interpretation. The retrieval setup is underspecified: how large are the narrative and episodic memories at evaluation time, what embedding similarity threshold or top-k is used, how are ties handled, and how sensitive are results to retrieval hyperparameters? The web retrieval pipeline is also potentially a major source of variance and hidden capability. What exactly is returned by Perplexica, how many documents/snippets are used, and are there safeguards against retrieving benchmark-specific solution text or leaked task descriptions? Since web search can be powerful but noisy, it would be useful to know latency, failure modes, and whether search quality differs across task categories. More broadly, because the system depends on proprietary backbones and external search, the practical reproducibility of the exact numbers is limited; the paper should acknowledge this more directly.

The ablation study is helpful but not fully convincing. It is conducted on a 65-example subset rather than the full benchmark, which is understandable for cost reasons, but the subset is small enough that some category-level conclusions may be unstable. No confidence intervals or significance estimates are provided. Some of the reported differences are large enough to be believable, but others are modest and could vary with sampling. In addition, the “w/o All” condition still seems to include ACI and perhaps other architectural changes relative to the baseline, so it is not a clean decomposition of where gains come from. The ACI ablation is described in text via a figure that is not numerically reproduced in the provided content, making it harder to assess. I would strongly prefer a clearer factorial breakdown on a fixed subset or, ideally, on the full benchmark for the most important comparisons: baseline, baseline+ACI, baseline+ACI+memory, full system.

The error analysis is a nice addition, but the methodology behind it is not sufficiently rigorous. The categories overlap, and a single task may contain multiple errors, so percentages are hard to interpret without knowing annotation protocol and inter-rater reliability. Were these labels assigned manually by the authors? If so, by how many annotators and with what agreement? Also, “execution error” is so broad that it risks becoming a catch-all category. A more fine-grained breakdown, perhaps separating repeated loops, premature DONE/FAIL, failure to recover from UI changes, and invalid action formatting, would be more actionable. Since the paper argues that ACI improves grounding and feedback, it would also be useful to quantify invalid-action rates, element-selection accuracy, or recovery after failed actions.

Another conceptual issue is the claim that the self-evaluator provides “textual rewards” analogous to hierarchical reinforcement learning. This analogy feels overstated. The system does not optimize a policy with reward signals in the RL sense; rather, it stores self-generated summaries for future retrieval. That is a reasonable memory mechanism, but calling it a reward process may confuse readers into expecting a stronger learning formulation than is actually present. I recommend simplifying this framing and describing the method more plainly as self-generated retrospective summaries used for retrieval augmentation.

The ACI design is one of the more interesting parts of the paper, but it would benefit from deeper analysis. The paper argues that augmenting the accessibility tree with OCR-derived text blocks is better than augmenting the image with tree information, yet there is no direct comparison isolating this choice. Likewise, the bounded primitive action space is intuitively appealing, but the paper does not quantify tradeoffs between expressivity and control granularity. For example, are there tasks that fail because the primitive set is too restrictive? How often does the center-click grounding heuristic cause failure? Since the error analysis identifies grounding and execution as dominant failure modes, a more detailed study of ACI design choices would strengthen the paper substantially.

I also noticed some presentation issues. There is duplicated Figure 2 content in the introduction. Some references appear duplicated or inconsistent, such as Fu et al. 2024a and 2024b both pointing to AutoGuide. The qualitative example is too thin in the main text to be informative; one screenshot and one click action do not really illustrate the hierarchical planning or memory usage. The paper would benefit from a full end-to-end example showing the manager’s subtasks, retrieved narrative/episodic memories, worker actions, and where replanning occurs. There are also occasional overclaims in the prose, such as “uses computers like a human,” which is rhetorically effective but scientifically imprecise given the low absolute success rates and heavy reliance on accessibility metadata unavailable to humans.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The benchmark gains are substantial, the system addresses a high-impact problem, and the architecture is plausible and useful. My overall assessment is positive but not unreservedly so. The strongest case for acceptance is as a solid empirical systems paper demonstrating that retrieval, hierarchical decomposition, and interface abstraction materially improve desktop agents. The weakest aspect is the ambiguity around evaluation protocol and memory construction, which affects the strength of the claims about generalization and learning.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following concrete revisions. First, clearly separate offline memory construction, online test-time adaptation, and evaluation, and report results for frozen-memory versus continually updated memory. Second, clarify whether benchmark initial states were used during exploration and provide a stricter no-benchmark-state memory condition. Third, add more implementation details for retrieval, search, prompting, and memory sizes. Fourth, provide statistical uncertainty for the ablations and, if possible, run the most important ablations on the full benchmark or a larger subset. Fifth, deepen the ACI analysis with direct comparisons of grounding variants and action-space choices. Sixth, tone down the RL analogy and novelty claims, and position the work more explicitly as an integrated architecture with strong empirical performance.

In summary, this is a strong and relevant paper with meaningful empirical improvements, but its claims would be much more convincing with tighter experimental protocol and clearer accounting of where the gains come from. If the conference values impactful agent systems work and is comfortable with some methodological ambiguity typical of fast-moving LLM-agent research, this paper is a credible acceptance candidate. If the bar is stricter on evaluation purity and algorithmic novelty, the current version falls somewhat short. My leaning is moderately positive, contingent on the authors addressing the concerns about memory construction and test-time adaptation.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper presents Agent S, an open framework for GUI-based computer control using multimodal LLMs. The system combines three main ideas: (1) experience-augmented hierarchical planning with a Manager that retrieves web knowledge and narrative memory to decompose tasks into subtasks, (2) Worker-level episodic memory retrieval and reflection for subtask execution, and (3) an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that uses screenshots plus an augmented accessibility tree and constrains actions to language-like GUI primitives. On OSWorld, Agent S improves over the reported GPT-4o baseline from 11.21% to 20.58% success rate, and it also improves over a comparable WindowsAgentArena baseline from 13.3% to 18.2%. The paper includes ablations on retrieval/memory components and ACI, plus qualitative error analysis.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: autonomous GUI agents for real computer use across diverse applications and operating systems.

The overall system design is intuitive and reasonably well motivated: hierarchical planning, retrieval from multiple memory levels, and a constrained interface are natural ingredients for long-horizon GUI control.
Strong empirical improvement on OSWorld relative to the cited baseline, with gains across multiple task categories and a new reported state of the art under the stated setup.
The ACI design is practically meaningful: combining screenshot reasoning with accessibility-tree grounding and restricting actions to valid primitives is a sensible engineering contribution.
Includes ablation studies attempting to isolate the effects of web knowledge, narrative memory, episodic memory, hierarchical planning, and ACI.
Cross-benchmark evaluation on WindowsAgentArena suggests some degree of transfer beyond the primary benchmark.
The paper is generally clear in describing the architecture and provides useful qualitative discussion and error categorization.
weaknesses: The main contribution is largely a systems integration paper; several ingredients (retrieval augmentation, hierarchical planning, memory, reflection, constrained action spaces, accessibility-tree grounding) are adapted from prior work, so the conceptual novelty is moderate.
Empirical performance, while improved, remains low in absolute terms (20.58% on OSWorld), which limits claims about robust autonomous computer use.

The evaluation protocol around memory construction and continual update raises concerns about fairness and possible benchmark contamination: the agent learns during inference and also bootstraps memory from tasks generated using benchmark environments, but the paper does not fully quantify overlap or leakage risk.

Ablations are conducted on a small sampled subset of 65 tasks rather than the full benchmark, making conclusions less stable; no confidence intervals, variance estimates, or repeated-run statistics are reported despite stochasticity from LLM agents and retrieval.

Comparisons may not be fully controlled: baselines differ not only in planning/memory but also in interface/action parameterization, OCR augmentation, and possibly prompting details, making attribution of gains difficult.

The self-evaluator is central to memory quality, yet its reliability is not rigorously validated; because it uses no ground truth or human feedback, it may store incorrect summaries and reinforce errors.

Claims of 'learning' and analogy to hierarchical reinforcement learning are overstated; the method is retrieval-augmented prompting with memory updates rather than optimization of a policy/value function.

The paper does not report efficiency metrics such as average steps, token usage, latency, or cost, which are especially important for practical GUI agents and for judging whether gains come from substantially more computation.

Generalization claims are limited because WindowsAgentArena evaluation still uses the same overall paradigm and only one comparable baseline; no analysis is given of how much memory/web retrieval contributes versus backbone/model differences or benchmark-specific artifacts.
methodological_flaws: Potential data leakage / contamination risk: initial memory construction uses environment-aware synthetic tasks derived from initial environments of OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena, and continual memory update occurs during inference. Without a strict protocol separating memory-building environments/tasks from evaluation tasks, the reported test performance may partially benefit from benchmark-specific exposure rather than true zero-shot generalization.

The paper frames the self-evaluation summaries as 'textual rewards' and draws an analogy to hierarchical reinforcement learning, but no reward optimization or RL objective is defined. This is a scientific-logic overclaim: retrieval-based memory accumulation is not equivalent to HRL in any formal sense presented here.

The formalism in Section 3 is mostly schematic and not mathematically substantive; there is no proof or theoretical argument supporting why the fusion/retrieval procedure should improve planning, nor analysis of retrieval quality, memory growth, or error propagation.

Empirical validity is weakened by lack of statistical rigor: no multiple seeds, no variance/error bars, and no significance testing are reported, despite highly stochastic agent behavior and small absolute success rates.

The ablation subset is small and manually stratified; because many category counts are tiny (e.g., OS has 6 tasks), percentage swings can be large and unstable. Strong causal claims about component importance are therefore not fully supported.

The comparison to baselines is not fully apples-to-apples. Agent S changes several factors simultaneously, including action abstraction, grounding representation, OCR augmentation, planning structure, and memory. As a result, the source of gains cannot be cleanly isolated from the main benchmark comparison.

The self-evaluator stores only trajectories deemed successful by the worker or summarized by an LLM judge, but the paper does not validate the precision/recall of these labels. This can introduce confirmation bias and noisy memory that may inflate or destabilize results.

The claim of broad generalizability across operating systems is stronger than warranted by a single additional benchmark with modest gains and no adaptation study, especially since both benchmarks share the same general GUI-agent evaluation style.
